cues.text: A Duchess Baptized at the Edge of Christendom

Ludmila was born around 860, likely near Melnik in Bohemia, and married Borivoj I while still a teenager — a marriage that placed her, without her choosing it, at the very frontier of Slavic Christianity.

Borivoj became the first Christian Duke of Bohemia, and tradition holds that he and Ludmila were baptized together around 871 by missionaries working in the tradition established by Sts. Cyril and Methodius.
Their recent mission to the Slavs had only just begun to take root east of the Frankish world.

Pagan resistance drove the couple briefly into exile, but they were soon recalled to rule, and after several more years on the throne resigned it in favor of their son Spytihnev and retired together to the fortress of Tetin.
A Grandmother's Charge

Spytihnev died only two years into his own reign, succeeded by his brother Vratislav, who married Drahomira — a woman later remembered by chroniclers as only a pretended Christian, secretly devoted to the old gods beneath a Christian veneer.
When Vratislav died in 921, still a young man, he left behind two small sons.
It was Ludmila, now in her sixties, who took on the formation of the elder, the boy who would become St. Wenceslaus .
She taught him, by every account, to read and to pray, and shaped in him the Christian conviction that would later cost him his own life at his brother's hands.
A Mother-in-Law's Jealousy

Ludmila's evident closeness to her grandson, and the real influence it gave her over Bohemia's future ruler, put her on a collision course with Drahomira, who as the boy's mother expected to govern the regency herself.

Chroniclers describe two women, both formidable, both aspiring to shape the same child's rule, in a rivalry that pagan nobles hostile to Christianity were only too glad to inflame on Drahomira's side.
Sensing the danger, Ludmila retired again to Tetin — the same fortress where she and Borivoj had once withdrawn together — but the retreat did not put her beyond reach.
Strangled With Her Own Veil
On September 15, 921, two noblemen dispatched by Drahomira broke into Tetin and murdered Ludmila, strangling her, according to the most consistent tradition, with her own veil.
The veil was a detail later readings would come to see as grimly fitting: an instrument of feminine modesty turned into a weapon.
She was buried hastily at Tetin, but Wenceslaus, once he came into his own power, had her remains solemnly translated to St. George's Basilica in Prague.
In the practice of the age, this act functioned as the formal recognition of her sanctity and was completed within four years of her death.
Legacy
Ludmila is remembered today as the first Bohemian woman whose life can be traced with any real historical confidence.

She is also remembered as the patroness of Bohemia, of converts, and — with a note of dark humor the Church has never shied from — of troubled relationships between mothers-in-law and daughters-in-law.
We recognize in her a grandmother whose most consequential act was neither political nor military but pedagogical: the patient, daily work of teaching a child to pray.
She carried out that work in the full knowledge that the people around her resented exactly what she was doing, and continued anyway until it cost her life.
